title: His Affection Cooled and He Turned Away, or His Companion Tired of Him
intro: Bashshar ibn Burd starts with a friend who has grown cold and asks whose drinking water is always clear. His night journey follows a wild ass and its mares to water where a hunter lies in wait, before the rider names his destination among Qays Aylan and joins its cavalry in the voice of the poem. The tribe fights for Marwan ibn Muhammad, the last Umayyad caliph in the East. Al-Abbasi names the patron as Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra of Qays, though the verses leave him unnamed. Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani later singled out the swords in a cloud of dust, showing how the movement of falling stars holds the whole comparison together.

translation: His affection cooled and he turned away, or his companion tired of him.
He only lowered himself by endlessly reproaching his friend.
1.sharh: We enter a friendship just as it comes apart. Either man may have tired of the other. What the speaker can see clearly is the indignity of continuing to demand an explanation.

translation: My two friends, do not marvel at love's burning,
or that a grieving man finds solace when those he loves are far away.
2.sharh: The conventional pair of companions hear two apparently contrary truths about absence. It raises the first pang of longing and can eventually wear that longing away.

translation: What his eye finds in Abda has healed him
of what his heart once suffered at the hands of its healers.
3.sharh: Abda is the beloved. The heart's “healers” are the women it has loved. The sight of Abda gives relief from a suffering for which those very healers were responsible.

translation: The headstrong heart has held back.
Only a touch of love sways it and comes to press its claim.
4.sharh: The heart has a will strong enough to call a halt. Love has only to touch it, though, to put it in motion again.

translation: If your brother is forever tasting one love after another,
his mounts turned towards every quarter,
5.sharh: The friend samples affections as someone might sample food. His riding camels already point in every direction before the speaker delivers his advice.

translation: then leave the way clear for him to go, and do not become
the mount of a restless traveller with so many ways to go.
6.sharh: The image turns back on the listener. If he makes himself the fickle friend's mount, he must carry the man wherever the man happens to choose.

translation: Your brother is the one who, if you doubt him, says,
“I gave you cause.” Reproach him and he meets you gently.
7.sharh: Instead of demanding proof when a friend grows suspicious, this man takes responsibility for having given offence. The two closely related Arabic verbs pass the doubt from one side to the other.

translation: If you take your friend to task for every fault,
you will never meet a friend you need not take to task.
8.sharh: The demand becomes impossible with the word “every”. The repeated verb of reproach lets the listener hear what such a friendship would sound like.

translation: Live alone, then, or keep faith with your brother.
Sometimes he commits a fault and sometimes he keeps clear of it.
9.sharh: Solitude is the logical price of demanding a faultless companion. The alternative allows one person to be capable both of the offence and of avoiding it.

translation: If you will not sometimes drink with specks on the water,
you will go thirsty. Whose drinking places always run clear?
10.sharh: A man at a water hole has quite a practical decision to make about a floating speck. The closing question puts the friend's failings back into proportion.

translation: Many a night so black that its daughters sleep,
its sons too, and its fosterlings, for dread of it,
11.sharh: A new scene opens after the maxims on friendship. The night is so formidable that even the creatures or people at home in it, its own extended family, have gone to sleep.

translation: I kept the sweetness of sleep from my eyes and my mount's
until the bands of darkness came undone.
12.sharh: Rider and mount keep the same vigil. At daybreak the darkness, imagined as bands wound over one another, gradually comes apart.

translation: At many a water hole you see sandgrouse feathers lying about,
its basin hidden, its stone lining still firm.
13.sharh: Dropped feathers are easier to see than the water itself. The hard slabs around its basin give the poet a second clue to a place a traveller might otherwise pass.

translation: Close to danger and far from any village,
a tireless worker through the night brought me there to drink.
14.sharh: What stands near the water is danger, and what stands far away is human help. The mount is credited with giving its rider a drink because its labour brought him there.

translation: A companion to night travel, no desert crossing twists
his long hind sinew or brings his flank veins to grief.
15.sharh: Two pieces of a camel's anatomy measure the ordeal more exactly than a general claim about speed. Neither the sinew running down the leg nor the vessels of the flank fail on the journey.

translation: Tall and of Ghurayri stock, his saddle timbers seem to ride
a wild ass with three mares, his brow bloodied by rival jacks.
16.sharh: The rider still sits on a pedigreed camel. Imagining its wooden saddletrees on an onager's back opens a second journey, that of the scarred male and his three females.

translation: Jealous over his company, he lets no outsider approach him,
and his companions look to none but him.
17.sharh: The male's jealousy keeps a rival away. The next half looks at the same small community from the females' side, all their expectation directed towards him.

translation: Once he has fed on good pasture he takes on another jack,
one moment biting in earnest, the next at play.
18.sharh: Good grazing gives the animal energy to spare. What starts as a trial of strength with another jack shifts between playful nipping and a real bite.

translation: A lean-flanked beast, he drove his sons from his daughters
at Dhu al-Radm, till no estrangement stirred among his mares.
19.sharh: Even his own sons are competitors once they grow up. Human words for kinship, jealousy and a change of heart continue the earlier meditation on the fickleness of affection.

translation: He and his mares grazed on green shoots for ninety nights,
with wild hemp to feed on and the meadow channels running.
20.sharh: Ninety nights give the good season a definite span. A particular plant eaten by onagers and the channels taking water out of the meadows make their former abundance tangible.

translation: Then the heat took power, and the ground's moisture was wrung out
by summer fire from a star whose blaze had kindled,
21.sharh: The speaker gives the heat dominion, then makes it wring the damp out of the soil. The rising of a summer star marks the seasonal change that will drive the herd to water.

translation: and the birds of the sandy flats flew up, while the tracks
put on great sheets of shimmering mirage,
22.sharh: Movement fills a landscape that has lost its water. The little creatures rising from the flats have also been understood as insects of the hot season. Below them mirage spreads like cloth.

translation: and the stud camel turned from the she-camels, and the hilltops
stood bare of all the gifts the rain had laid there,
23.sharh: The heat interrupts the breeding life of the camels and strips the high ground. The previous season's growth had seemed a gift deposited there for safekeeping.

translation: and the oryx took shelter in shade, and the grass awns sped away,
driven by a loud summer wind whose companies came at a trot,
24.sharh: At one end of the scale a full-grown oryx seeks stillness. At the other a tiny awn is carried headlong by gusts imagined as ranks of trotting riders.

translation: the herd came at morning complaining of thirst with their eyes
to the sturdy jack, though they could not speak to him.
25.sharh: The long sentence that began with the onset of summer finally reaches its consequence. The females' looks do the work of speech and put the decision in the male's hands.

translation: He stood on high ground weighing his course.
Should he go to water early or make for it by night?
26.sharh: On a rise the male weighs one time for reaching water against another. The rare verb at the rhyme is uncertain in transmission, but the herd's eventual choice is made clear in the next lines.

translation: When the face of resolve showed itself and a face
of night startled him, the night traveller turned to water.
27.sharh: Resolve and darkness each present a face to him. The final word identifies him more precisely than “traveller”: he is one who sets out by night specifically to reach water.

translation: All night, while darkness hid their bodies,
he raced them for the heart of the track, and they raced him.
28.sharh: Their shapes disappear, but the reciprocal verbs keep each animal in the race. To win is to seize the best part of the track from the others.

translation: Whenever they bounded across the night's wilderness he drew them in
to a track whose clear course shone like the Milky Way,
29.sharh: The herd's bounding threatens to scatter it. He brings it back to a continuous pale line on the ground, with the Milky Way for its counterpart overhead.

translation: until among the sandgrouse they found a way down
to water ringed on every side by dangers.
30.sharh: The birds lead them to a place where they can actually descend and drink. The approach is narrow in another sense too, since the speaker has already seen the dangers about it.

translation: There is a clamour of birds rushing in one flight after another,
loud as the grasshoppers on a day of fierce heat.
31.sharh: The feathers were silent markers from a distance. Close to the water the flocks arrive in audible succession, the sound carrying the heat of the day into the scene.

translation: He brought his mares to the side of the stream, his eye
searching this way and that, while someone in a hide was watching him.
32.sharh: The jack is both watcher and watched. We are shown the hunter's hiding place before the hunter himself is described.

translation: A man with a matched set of blue-tipped arrows and a supple yellow bow
that tugs against a tightly twisted string which tugs back.
33.sharh: The hunter first appears as the colours of his equipment. Bow and string are given equal parts in a struggle of opposing pulls.

translation: When it gives its low call it moans, and the echo moans back,
as one sick man groans an answer to another.
34.sharh: The note of the bow comes back off the landscape. Its echo has the particular helplessness of an invalid who can answer another's groan only by groaning in turn.

translation: It is as if wealth had sworn a solemn oath
never to come near him except for what his bow brings near.
35.sharh: Wealth is made a person who has sworn to keep his distance. The double use of “near” measures the hunter's livelihood against the reach of his bow.

translation: He goes home to the mother of two girls. It weighs on him
if he comes to her empty-handed, or she raises her voice against him.
36.sharh: The hunter has a household waiting for him. The two daughters change what the reader knows about the shot he is about to take.

translation: Then as the jack went down into the stream, deceived
by the burning of his thirst about a hunter who would not spring at him,
37.sharh: Earlier he searched the bank with his eyes. Now the need to drink overrides his caution, and the hunter's stillness gives him no last warning.

translation: the hunter shot. The arrow passed grazing his belly
and the base of his throat. He wheeled away with death hard upon him.
38.sharh: The subject switches from animal to man at the instant of shooting and back again when the animal bolts. The light verb “grazing” momentarily conceals the harm done.

translation: He struck stones that bruised the length of his neck.
There lay the two props for his sides and the one that drew his blood.
39.sharh: The rocks prop the fallen animal up as if resting him on cushions. One also opens the flow of blood. The story of the wild ass ends with this cruel transformation of the stones.

translation: My companion fears death if I set out,
as if death were kin to him when he stays at home.
40.sharh: The rider's travelling companion reappears after the long animal episode. For home to guarantee safety, death itself would have to grant the man a relative's favour.

translation: I told him that a stay in Iraq
is unhealthy when its south winds blow against you.
41.sharh: Iraq is the companion's present home. The traditional association between the south wind and illness gives him a reason nearer than the dangers of distant travel.

translation: Perhaps, by travelling through the dark, you will bring within reach
a trustworthy brother whose good qualities will do you good,
42.sharh: The traveller weighs a possible benefit against his companion's certain fear. A brother is someone whose qualities can be felt in the help he gives.

translation: one of the people of Qays, Qays Aylan.
They are generosity's springs, from which its very clouds are watered.
43.sharh: The dependable brother now has a tribal address. In a reversal of the ordinary water cycle, the clouds that bring gifts must first draw water from the springs of Qays.

translation: Let the needy man who has been denied everything tie his cords
to theirs, and the things he longs for are driven to him.
44.sharh: The impoverished man's tie to his protectors becomes visible as ropes joined together. What he desired then comes to him as readily as a herd driven to his door.

translation: And on many a day of Sirius, when the heat ran wild,
its blaze so great that no man drinking water could quench his thirst,
45.sharh: The rising of Sirius belongs to the season of extreme heat. The speaker repeats himself as if to decide whether to blame the day or the flame that has taken possession of it.

translation: I lifted my saddle onto a long-striding mount
that sped along, its rider high as if on a tree trunk,
46.sharh: The camel is at once a swift-moving animal and something as substantial as a standing trunk. The rider feels the height as well as the speed.

translation: through a grey wilderness that made figures dance, a place to lose one's way,
its water holes unknown and its level reaches uncharted,
47.sharh: The flicker of desert air makes even stationary figures seem to dance. Open level ground offers little comfort to a rider who cannot locate its water.

translation: to meet the sons of Aylan. The great undertakings in their deeds
rise higher than anything that others do.
48.sharh: The purpose of the difficult ride arrives at last. Even their achievements are spoken of as things one mounts, carrying a word from the journey into the praise.

translation: Those men with their swords cut away the blindness
that covered error, until the seeker could see the truth.
49.sharh: The speaker gives political allegiance the language of right and error. The sword clears an obstruction to sight so that the seeker can see which side to take.

translation: When they ride with Mashrafi swords and spears,
and Marwan's mounted companies are being counted in the morning,
50.sharh: The Umayyad caliph Marwan ibn Muhammad is now named. Counting his successive companies gives the reader some idea of scale before the poet asks his question.

translation: what rebel, what tribe,
what great host would not leave its kindred weeping?
51.sharh: The consequence of mobilising the army is expressed as a question about the mourners it will make. The last term can denote a great host or, as Ibn Ashur suggests here, a rash man.

translation: Wait a little. Our fine horses whinny in Iraq.
You can almost see al-Dahhak's mourner already on his feet.
52.sharh: The Kharijite leader al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Shaybani comes into view as the army's particular adversary. The noise of horses is already, in the speaker's imagination, the sound before a funeral.

translation: Many a man has reached up against Marwan, with a choking obstacle before him
and terror like the deep sea when its wave crests surge,
53.sharh: A threat to the caliph is described first in the throat, as an obstacle one cannot swallow, then on the scale of a storm sea. The next line supplies the enemy's fate.

translation: and the mother of deaths has lodged her daughters with him
by means of our swords. We are the ruin of those we fight.
54.sharh: Death has a household and can billet her daughters on the man who threatened Marwan. The speaker has made the tribe's weapons his own.

translation: One of us has always held a city on watch
or a frontier post where the enemy's governors are feared.
55.sharh: The claim extends from civil government to frontier duty. The Persian title marzban recalls the border rulers against whom a garrison might have to hold out.

translation: When a tyrant king turns his cheek away in pride,
we go to him with swords and remonstrate.
56.sharh: The verb of friendly reproach from the opening returns. Addressed with swords to a king too proud to look at anyone, its old courtesy takes on a grim edge.

translation: When the enemy crept forward in fear of our anger
and watched us out in the open, we did not wait to watch him.
57.sharh: The enemy advances warily and waits for signs of what Qays will do. The tribe answers his watchfulness with the open approach described next.

translation: We rode out to him openly with every straightened lance
and bright sword whose striking edges thirsted for blood.
58.sharh: The thirsty edge of the blade recalls the earlier need for water. The metaphor transfers that need from the hunted animal to the metal carried by men.

translation: Many a host, dark as the coming of night, shook with its numbers,
with its camels and Khatti spears red at the shafts below their heads.
59.sharh: The host is dark in the mass, but a flash of red is visible where the heads of the spears meet the shafts. The word otherwise familiar as “foxes” names that part of a spear.

translation: We went against it while the sun was still in her mother's chamber
peeping at us, before a drop of dew had melted and run,
60.sharh: A shy girl looking out of her mother's private room and dew still resting on the ground mark the same early hour. The battle begins before either scene of awakening is complete.

translation: with blows whose taste was death to whoever tasted them,
and whose disgrace caught up with the man whom flight had saved.
61.sharh: The man who stays learns the flavour of the blow. The man who escapes only discovers that the dishonour of flight has kept pace with him.

translation: The dust raised over their heads and our swords within it
were like a night in which the stars came tumbling down.
62.sharh: Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani reads the two halves as a single moving picture. The swords flash at different angles and vanish into the dust, as falling stars flare and go out in the dark.

translation: We sent sudden death among them. We are
the sons of kingship, its strips of banner cloth beating above us.
63.sharh: The attackers claim descent from royal power itself. What the eye can verify of this claim is the royal cloth snapping over their heads.

translation: By evening one part of them was in chains and as many
lay dead. Of another part the fugitives sought refuge in the great river.
64.sharh: The repeated proportions dispose of the defeated in three groups. Ibn Ashur identifies the great water to which the last group fled as the Euphrates.

translation: And many a vast host whose gleaming iron veiled the sun,
its battalions snatching the very sight from armoured warriors,
65.sharh: The same mass of iron can block light and throw it back in a blinding flash. Even the seasoned men facing the host lose command of their own sight.

translation: The open earth could scarcely swallow it when it marched.
Its shoulders jostled against the buttresses of the mountains.
66.sharh: The plain has a throat that can barely take this army, and the army has shoulders. Its ranks are measured against the physical bulk of mountains.

translation: Its two battle flanks seemed
Shamam and Salma, or Aja and its neighbouring Kawakib.
67.sharh: Named mountains give the two wings of the army a real profile. Here Kawakib is identified in the diwan as a mountain near Aja. A few lines earlier the same word meant the stars.

translation: With that host we left Kalb and Qahtan seeking
someone to shelter them from death whose squadrons bore down on them.
68.sharh: Kalb and Qahtan name the tribal opponents. Death takes on the cavalry formations of the attacking host, while its targets are reduced to seeking another man's protection.

translation: Once bridled, our horses laid Damascus open,
and the dupe of Hims reaped his reversals there.
69.sharh: Damascus and Hims begin the poem's roll of places. The man it calls deluded is identified in the diwan as Thabit ibn Nu'aym of Judham, soon to appear by name.

translation: Our horses reached Palestine, and its host broke and ran
from a moving storm cloud whose pelting rain was death.
70.sharh: The enemy appears to see a weather front moving across the sky. What its wind drives against the fugitives is lethal, transforming the familiar storm of the desert crossing.

translation: A turn of the fighting fell from us upon Palmyra too.
So do the visitations of war come round from every side.
71.sharh: Palmyra, or Tadmur, receives its turn after the other Syrian and Palestinian places. The word for its ordeal also means one's turn in a succession.

translation: It comes again with a spirit that does not slip from guidance
as Thabit and his kin strayed from it.
72.sharh: The returning force carries its leader's loyalty with it. There is an irony in branding a man named Thabit, “steadfast”, as the one who swerved.

translation: Thabit openly called Ibn Simak to the erring cause,
and his experiences gave his sons no guidance.
73.sharh: Thabit's appeal to Ibn Simak is made publicly. His family, the speaker thinks, ought to have read a warning in their father's experience.

translation: He called on Sa'id and drew down a bucketful of misery
as the last of his misfortunes poured down on him.
74.sharh: Sa'id is identified as a son of the Umayyad caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. Misfortune is a well from which a man draws a brimming bucket, and the two rhyme-like nouns let one pouring answer another.

translation: How strange the exertions of Ibn Aghnam among them,
and of Uthman. Time indeed is full of marvels.
75.sharh: The poet adds two more names to his list of astonishing choices. Ibn Ashur could not securely identify Ibn Aghnam, and the verse preserves no further clue to his identity.

translation: Each was borne flying on a fine mount, a whole man,
and his finger joints flew to the dogs.
76.sharh: The same verb carries each man past twice. First he flies by on a fine camel, then parts of his body fly in pieces, the old distinction disintegrating with the rider.

translation: We gave the order early in the day and they were put on crosses.
By evening Hamid's executioner was hewing the trunk for him.
77.sharh: A day of punishment is measured from the morning order to the evening labour of one man. For Hamid, the trunk taking shape says what is about to happen.

translation: Ibn Ruh submitted to the community.
When we roared at him, his locks stood up in fear.
78.sharh: The roar is sufficient to bring Ibn Ruh over to the caliph's party. The hairs rising on his head make fear visible before he has had to speak.

translation: At pregnant Kufa we brought our horses against them,
bringing on death's vanguard. We were the men who brought it.
79.sharh: Kufa is imagined as a city carrying upheaval within it. Death approaches in military order, its advance party arriving with the horses.

translation: We made its women gather over this man and that
in mourning assemblies. One called for weeping and another answered.
80.sharh: The clamour of cavalry gives way to women calling across groups of mourners. A death here and another there meet in a communal response.

translation: Widows and wives. In their sorrow its fine women seemed
the white gazelles of the open plain and its herds of wild cattle.
81.sharh: The poem makes room for both women who have lost husbands and married women who have come to mourn. Desert animals, formerly seen in their own story, return as figures for the mourners.

translation: They wept over a man straight and sharp as a spearhead
whom death overtook at our hands. They were his mourners.
82.sharh: Giving a fallen opponent the qualities of a spear point heightens the victor's claim. The women now perform the lament predicted for al-Dahhak earlier.

translation: When, with the caliph, we had taken our satisfaction from them,
and he had struck through us until his purposes were fulfilled,
83.sharh: The sentence waits for the next line to disclose the army's new direction. It first defines the partnership between a caliph seeking his ends and a tribe claiming its revenge.

translation: we advanced against al-Dahhak, dealing in death,
Marwan's claws still bloody from Judham.
84.sharh: The campaign turns back to the Kharijite leader. Marwan is a beast still carrying the blood of the tribe of Judham on its claws as it approaches another foe.

translation: We had made ready a lion and a black snake shedding its skin,
so many deaths for anyone whose scorpions crept our way.
85.sharh: A lion and a sloughing black snake figure the forces in reserve. The enemy sent towards them was already figured as a creature with a sting.

translation: Al-Dahhak has come to be just another Thabit.
He disobeyed us, so we sent Death to invite him to a feast.
86.sharh: Thabit's fate supplies the prediction for al-Dahhak. The verb belongs to an invitation to dine, making Death the messenger of a savagely courteous last line.

1.1.3.head: اِزوَرَّ
1.1.3.meaning: To turn aside or draw away from someone.

2.1.4.head: لَوعَة
2.1.4.meaning: An inward burning of grief or longing.

2.2.2.head: سَلوَة
2.2.2.meaning: Relief when the heart ceases to dwell on a love or grief.

3.1.5.head: عَبدَة
3.1.5.meaning: Abda, the beloved whom Bashshar names in several poems.

3.2.5.head: طَبيبَة
3.2.5.meaning: Women healers, here women whom the lover credits with soothing his distress.

4.1.1.head: أَقصَرَ
4.1.1.meaning: To desist from a course on which one had set out.

4.1.2.head: عِرزام
4.1.2.meaning: Headstrong or of powerful resolve, applied to the lover's heart.

5.1.3.head: ذَوّاق
5.1.3.meaning: Forever sampling, here a person whose affection flits from one attachment to another.

5.2.4.head: أَوب
5.2.4.meaning: A quarter or direction of travel.

5.2.5.head: رَكيبَة
5.2.5.meaning: A riding camel, here a whole company of mounts ready for departure.

6.2.1.head: مَطِيَّة
6.2.1.meaning: A mount used on a journey.

7.1.4.head: رابَ
7.1.4.meaning: Here to suspect one's friend or doubt his conduct.

7.2.1.head: أَرابَ
7.2.1.meaning: To give cause for suspicion. The friend accepts that he has done so.

7.2.4-5.head: لانَ جانِبُه
7.2.4-5.meaning: “His side grew soft”, meaning he responded without harshness.

9.2.1.head: قارَفَ
9.2.1.meaning: To engage in or commit an act, especially a fault.

10.1.7.head: القَذى
10.1.7.meaning: Small specks or motes that float on water or get into the eye.

11.2.4.head: رَبيبَة
11.2.4.meaning: A fosterling. Night's fosterlings are those brought up in its company.

12.2.5.head: عِصابَة
12.2.5.meaning: A band or wrapping, the plural here evoking layers of darkness.

13.1.4.head: الغَطاط
13.1.4.meaning: Ghatat, a kind of sandgrouse whose presence can show a traveller where to find water.

13.1.5.head: جَوّ
13.1.5.meaning: The space around or within a site, here the ground about the water.

13.2.2.head: الحَيا
13.2.2.meaning: Haya, the water basin in this reading. A variant, jaba, means the collected water or part of its basin.

13.2.6.head: نَصيبَة
13.2.6.meaning: A slab set around a basin to close the gaps. The reciter has nada'ibuhu with a dad. Ibn Ashur identifies that spelling in the manuscript as an error for nasa'ibuhu with a sad.

14.1.3.head: تَغرير
14.1.3.meaning: Exposure to danger or the risk of destruction.

14.2.5.head: دائِب
14.2.5.meaning: One who keeps working or travelling without slackening.

15.1.5.head: مَفازَة
15.1.5.meaning: A tract of open, perilous desert.

15.2.1.head: نَسا
15.2.1.meaning: The long tendon or vessel extending from hip to heel in older anatomy.

15.2.5.head: حالِب
15.2.5.meaning: A vessel along the flank. Older descriptions speak of a pair running from the back towards the belly.

16.1.2.head: غُرَيرِيّ
16.1.2.meaning: Ghurayri, of the prized Ghurayr stock of camels.

16.1.4.head: قَتَد
16.1.4.meaning: A wooden piece of the camel's saddletree.

16.2.2.head: مُثلَث
16.2.2.meaning: A male onager attended by three females.

16.2.5.head: أَحقَب
16.2.5.meaning: A wild ass with a pale belly, here the rival males.

17.2.1.head: خَليط
17.2.1.meaning: One who mixes with others, here a rival entering the herd.

18.1.4.head: سَنّ
18.1.4.meaning: Good grazing. The dual suggests the abundance the animal has enjoyed.

18.1.6.head: مِسحَل
18.1.6.meaning: A male wild ass or jack.

18.2.3.head: تَعذام
18.2.3.meaning: Biting or nipping with the teeth.

19.1.1.head: أَقَبّ
19.1.1.meaning: Lean in the belly and flanks.

19.2.1-2.head: ذو الرَّضم
19.2.1-2.meaning: Dhu al-Radm, a place name. Radm denotes rocks piled together.

19.2.6.head: ثالِبَة
19.2.6.meaning: A female turning against her companion, in the diwan commentator's explanation.

20.2.2.head: أَبَق
20.2.2.meaning: A wild hemp-like plant whose seed onagers feed on.

20.2.5.head: مِذنَب
20.2.5.meaning: An outlet that takes a meadow's water into another channel or meadow.

21.1.3.head: الحَرّ
21.1.3.meaning: Summer heat in the recorded text. One proposed reading means the animals' ability to go without water on green fodder.

22.1.2-3.head: عَصافيرُ الشَّقائِق
22.1.2-3.meaning: “Birds of the sandy flats.” Other explanations identify insects audible in the heat, or windblown anemone petals.

22.2.2.head: الآل
22.2.2.meaning: A mirage, especially the shimmering that seems to lift distant objects.

22.2.4.head: مُلاءَة
22.2.4.meaning: A broad cloth or wrap, here in the plural.

23.1.3.head: شائِل
23.1.3.meaning: A she-camel that raises her tail for a male, also one whose milk has diminished after calving.

23.1.4.head: قَريع
23.1.4.meaning: A stud camel selected for breeding.

23.2.2.head: صَمد
23.2.2.meaning: A rise of firm ground or a low hill.

23.2.5.head: مَوهِبَة
23.2.5.meaning: A gift, here the rain and the growth it leaves on the hills.

24.1.2.head: المَها
24.1.2.meaning: The Arabian oryx, a white desert antelope.

24.1.4.head: اِستَوفَضَ
24.1.4.meaning: To hasten or make something hurry, here dry plant matter driven by wind.

24.1.5.head: السَّفا
24.1.5.meaning: Awns, the fine bristles of seed heads.

24.2.4.head: خَبَّ
24.2.4.meaning: To trot or go at a quick pace.

25.1.5.head: الصَّدى
25.1.5.meaning: Burning thirst. The word can also mean an echo, a sense used later in the poem.

25.2.2.head: الجَأب
25.2.2.meaning: A sturdy, powerful wild ass, here the jack leading the herd.

26.1.3.head: عَلياء
26.1.3.meaning: A height with a view of the surrounding country.

26.2.2.head: وِرد
26.2.2.meaning: The act or appointed time of going to water.

26.2.5.head: واتَبَ
26.2.5.meaning: A difficult transmitted verb. The diwan commentator connects it with going to water by night, the alternative to an early visit.

27.1.4.head: زِماع
27.1.4.meaning: A firm intention to set out.

27.2.6.head: قارِب
27.2.6.meaning: One travelling by night to reach a watering place.

28.2.1.head: ناهَبَ
28.2.1.meaning: To race someone for something, here as if snatching the road away from a rival.

28.2.2-3.head: أُمُّ الهُدى
28.2.2-3.meaning: “Mother of guidance”, the guiding middle or main course of a clear track.

29.2.4.head: المَجَرَّة
29.2.4.meaning: The Milky Way, whose luminous band resembles a clear path.

29.2.5.head: لاحِب
29.2.5.meaning: An open, well-marked stretch of road.

30.1.6.head: شَريعَة
30.1.6.meaning: An accessible approach or slope down to water.

31.1.3.head: مُستَوفِضَة
31.1.3.meaning: Rushing at speed, here the flocks of sandgrouse coming to drink.

31.1.5.head: الوَلى
31.1.5.meaning: Succession, one flight coming hard upon the next.

31.2.6.head: جُندَب
31.2.6.meaning: A grasshopper or similar heat-loving insect.

33.1.2.head: صيغَة
33.1.2.meaning: A matched set of arrows from one maker.

33.1.3.head: أَزرَق
33.1.3.meaning: Blue, here the metallic colour of the arrowheads.

33.1.4.head: صَفراء
33.1.4.meaning: A yellow bow, named by the colour of its wood.

33.2.2.head: مُستَحصِد
33.2.2.meaning: Tightly twisted, here the taut bowstring.

34.1.2.head: رَزَمَ
34.1.2.meaning: To make a low moaning sound, originally of a camel.

36.1.1.head: آلَ
36.1.1.meaning: To return or come home to.

36.1.5.head: آدَ
36.1.5.meaning: To weigh heavily upon or burden someone.

37.2.1-2.head: غَليلُ الحَشا
37.2.1-2.meaning: “The burning of the vitals”, the inward fire of thirst.

37.2.4.head: قانِص
37.2.4.meaning: A hunter lying in wait for game.

38.2.1.head: لَبَّة
38.2.1.meaning: The hollow at the base of the throat. The recitation uses a plural where Ibn Ashur's main text has a singular.

38.2.2.head: اِنصاعَ
38.2.2.meaning: To wheel round and dart away.

38.2.4.head: كَرَبَ
38.2.4.meaning: To draw very near or press hard upon someone.

39.1.3.head: رَدَعَ
39.1.3.meaning: To check or strike back, here stones abruptly stopping the animal's flight.

39.1.4.head: نَضِيّ
39.1.4.meaning: The stretch of neck between shoulder and ear.

39.2.3.head: عامِر
39.2.3.meaning: A support for the side of someone too weak to sit unaided, here two stones against the animal's flanks.

39.2.4.head: شاخِب
39.2.4.meaning: Something that makes blood spurt, interpreted here as the stone that opened a vessel.

40.1.2.head: مَنِيَّة
40.1.2.meaning: Death, or one of the ways death is appointed to come.

41.2.1.head: وَخيم
41.2.1.meaning: Unhealthy or detrimental to one who stays there.

41.2.5.head: جَنوب
41.2.5.meaning: A south wind, here with the less familiar plural jana'ib.

42.1.2.head: اِستَدنى
42.1.2.meaning: To bring or seek to bring within reach.

42.2.1-2.head: أَخو ثِقَة
42.2.1-2.meaning: “A brother of trust”, a man one can rely on.

42.2.5.head: مَنقَبَة
42.2.5.meaning: A recognised merit or quality worthy of honour.

43.1.4-5.head: قَيسُ عَيلان
43.1.4-5.meaning: Qays Aylan, a large northern Arab tribal grouping that included Uqayl, Bashshar's patrons by clientage.

43.2.2.head: النَّدى
43.2.2.meaning: Generosity, also dew, a double sense sustained by the springs and clouds.

44.1.2.head: مُجحِد
44.1.2.meaning: Reduced to poverty or narrow means.

44.2.4.head: رَغيبَة
44.2.4.meaning: Something much desired, especially a valuable gift.

45.1.2.head: عَبورِيّ
45.1.2.meaning: Aburi, associated by Ibn Ashur with Sirius, the Dog Star, and the heat of its rising.

45.2.1.head: لَظى
45.2.1.meaning: Flame or the blazing intensity of heat.

46.1.3.head: رَحل
46.1.3.meaning: A camel saddle and riding gear.

46.2.1.head: زَفَّ
46.2.1.meaning: To move rapidly with quick steps, as an ostrich runs.

46.2.5.head: جِذل
46.2.5.meaning: A tree trunk or stump, here an image of the camel's height and solidity.

47.1.1.head: أَغبَر
47.1.1.meaning: A dusty or grey tract. The recording introduces it with “through”, while Ibn Ashur prints “and”.

47.1.4.head: مَضِلَّة
47.1.4.meaning: A region where it is easy to lose one's way.

47.2.3.head: سَبسَب
47.2.3.meaning: An extensive stretch of open, level desert.

48.1.3.head: عَيلان
48.1.3.meaning: Aylan, the ancestral name in Qays Aylan. His “sons” here are the tribes already praised as Qays.

48.2.5.head: مَركَب
48.2.5.meaning: A great undertaking, literally something a person mounts or braves.

49.1.1.head: أُلاكَ
49.1.1.meaning: An older form of ula'ika, “those men”.

50.1.3.head: المَشرَفِيَّة
50.1.3.meaning: Mashrafi swords, named for places called Masharif on or near the Syrian frontier.

50.1.4.head: قَناة
50.1.4.meaning: A lance or lance shaft, here plural.

50.2.2.head: مَروان
50.2.2.meaning: Marwan ibn Muhammad, the last Umayyad caliph in the eastern empire, killed in 132 AH (750 CE).

51.2.1.head: أَرعَن
51.2.1.meaning: An immense host, also a rash or foolish man. The latter sense has been proposed at this point.

52.1.1.head: رُوَيداً
52.1.1.meaning: Wait a little, here with the sense of a threat.

52.2.2.head: الضَّحّاك
52.2.2.meaning: Al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Shaybani, a Kharijite leader who took Kufa and opposed Marwan ibn Muhammad.

52.2.5.head: نادِب
52.2.5.meaning: A mourner who raises a lament for the dead.

53.1.1.head: سَما
53.1.1.meaning: To rise or aspire, here to challenge the caliph.

53.1.5.head: الشَّجا
53.1.5.meaning: Something lodged in the throat, here an almost insuperable obstacle.

53.2.2.head: لُجّ
53.2.2.meaning: The deep, turbulent main body of the sea.

53.2.5.head: غارِب
53.2.5.meaning: A crest, here the crests of waves.

54.1.1.head: أَحَلَّ
54.1.1.meaning: To bring someone to lodge or settle in a place.

55.2.3.head: ثَغر
55.2.3.meaning: A frontier post exposed to enemy incursions.

55.2.5.head: مَرزُبان
55.2.5.meaning: Marzban, a Persian governor or warden of a frontier.

56.1.4-5.head: صَعَّرَ خَدَّهُ
56.1.4-5.meaning: “He turned his cheek aside”, a gesture of arrogance or disdain.

57.1.5.head: سُخط
57.1.5.meaning: Anger or displeasure, here feared by the enemy.

58.2.1.head: أَبيَض
58.2.1.meaning: A bright steel sword, literally “a white one”.

58.2.4.head: مَضرِب
58.2.4.meaning: The striking part of a sword blade.

59.1.2.head: جُنح
59.1.2.meaning: A portion of night, particularly its gathering darkness.

59.1.5.head: حَصى
59.1.5.meaning: Pebbles, also a count or the multitude counted.

59.2.2.head: الخَطِّيّ
59.2.2.meaning: Khatti, spears named for al-Khatt, a trading place on the eastern Arabian coast.

59.2.4.head: ثَعلَب
59.2.4.meaning: The end of a spear shaft that fits into its iron head.

60.2.2.head: الطَّلّ
60.2.2.meaning: Dew, or a very fine rain, here drops that have yet to run.

61.2.5.head: مَثلَبَة
61.2.5.meaning: A cause of disgrace or reproach.

62.1.2-3.head: مُثارُ النَّقع
62.1.2-3.meaning: “The stirring up of the dust”, the cloud raised over the field by the horses and the army.

62.2.3.head: تَهاوى
62.2.3.meaning: To fall one after another from different points.

63.1.4.head: فُجاءَة
63.1.4.meaning: Suddenness, as in an unannounced death.

63.2.5.head: سَبيبَة
63.2.5.meaning: A strip of cloth, here one of the streamers of the royal standards.

64.2.4.head: البَحر
64.2.4.meaning: A great expanse of water, identified in the diwan as the Euphrates.

65.1.1.head: أَرعَن
65.1.1.meaning: A host so vast that it resembles a mountain.

66.2.2.head: رُكن
66.2.2.meaning: A strong side or buttress, here the projecting sides of mountains.

67.1.2.head: جَنابَة
67.1.2.meaning: A flank of an army. The dual denotes its right and left wings.

67.1.4.head: خَمِس
67.1.4.meaning: The army, understood as a metrical shortening of khamis. Ibn Ashur also proposes hamis, “fierce”, in his textual note.

67.1.5.head: الوَغى
67.1.5.meaning: The din of battle, hence battle itself.

67.2.1.head: شَمام
67.2.1.meaning: Shamam, a mountain traditionally located in the Yamama region.

67.2.2.head: سَلمى
67.2.2.meaning: Salma, one of the two mountains of Tayyi' in northern Arabia, paired with Aja.

67.2.4.head: أَجا
67.2.4.meaning: Aja, the other of the two mountains of Tayyi', traditionally named with Salma.

67.2.5.head: كَواكِب
67.2.5.meaning: Kawakib, a mountain near Aja in the diwan commentary.

68.1.3.head: كَلب
68.1.3.meaning: Kalb, a tribe of Quda'a with considerable influence in Syria.

68.1.4.head: قَحطان
68.1.4.meaning: Qahtan, the traditional ancestor of the southern Arabian tribes and here a name for the tribes themselves.

68.2.5.head: مِقنَب
68.2.5.meaning: A troop of horsemen or horses.

69.1.2.head: دِمَشق
69.1.2.meaning: Damascus, capital of Umayyad Syria and seat of the caliphate before Marwan's move to Harran.

69.2.3-4.head: مَغرورُ حِمص
69.2.3-4.meaning: “The dupe of Hims”, identified by Ibn Ashur as Thabit ibn Nu'aym of Judham, an opponent of Marwan. Hims is modern Homs.

70.1.2.head: فِلِسطين
70.1.2.meaning: Filastin, the military district of Palestine in Umayyad Syria.

70.2.2.head: عارِض
70.2.2.meaning: A bank of cloud barring the horizon.

70.2.5.head: حاصِب
70.2.5.meaning: A wind pelting the ground with stones.

71.1.4.head: تَدمُر
71.1.4.meaning: Tadmur, the oasis city of Palmyra in the Syrian desert.

71.2.2.head: عُروض
71.2.2.meaning: Ways or quarters from which something may come.

71.2.4.head: عَرا
71.2.4.meaning: To visit or come down upon someone.

72.2.4.head: ثابِت
72.2.4.meaning: Thabit ibn Nu'aym of Judham, leader of a Syrian revolt against Marwan.

73.1.2-3.head: اِبنُ سِماك
73.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Simak, an ally summoned by Thabit and associated in the commentary with Kalb.

74.1.2.head: سَعيد
74.1.2.meaning: Sa'id ibn Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, an Umayyad prince named here as a rebel ally.

74.1.3.head: اِستَصَبَّ
74.1.3.meaning: To draw a pouring for oneself, here a draught of misery.

74.2.1.head: ذَنوب
74.2.1.meaning: A large bucket filled with water, hence a share or portion.

75.1.4-5.head: اِبنُ أَغنَم
75.1.4-5.meaning: Ibn Aghnam, a named rebel whom Ibn Ashur could not identify.

75.2.1.head: عُثمان
75.2.1.meaning: Uthman, identified in the diwan commentary as Uthman ibn Sa'id ibn Hisham.

76.2.4.head: راجِبَة
76.2.4.meaning: A joint of a finger, here plural.

77.2.2.head: حَميد
77.2.2.meaning: Hamid, another of the defeated men. The verse does not securely establish his full identity.

78.1.1.head: باطَ
78.1.1.meaning: To be humbled after holding power, hence to submit. The printed diwan reads wanata, “and he attached [himself]”.

78.1.2-3.head: اِبنُ رَوح
78.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Ruh, tentatively identified in the diwan as Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Ruh ibn Zinba' of Judham.

78.2.4.head: ذُؤابَة
78.2.4.meaning: A forelock or tress of hair.

79.1.1.head: الكوفَة
79.1.1.meaning: Kufa, the Iraqi city on the Euphrates that became a base for al-Dahhak.

79.2.2.head: رَعيل
79.2.2.meaning: The leading body of cavalry or a mounted advance guard.

80.1.5.head: نِساء
80.1.5.meaning: Women. The recorded feminine suffix refers back to Kufa. Ibn Ashur has the masculine suffix, referring the women to each fallen man.

80.2.1.head: مَأتَم
80.2.1.meaning: An assembly, especially of women gathered to mourn.

81.1.1.head: أَيِّم
81.1.1.meaning: A woman without a husband, here including women widowed in the fighting.

81.1.4.head: نَهِيَّة
81.1.4.meaning: A fine, well-grown she-camel, used here of the fine women in the gathering.

81.2.2.head: الحُزن
81.2.2.meaning: Grief, the sense given in the recording’s gloss. With a different first vowel the word could also denote the rough ground where gazelles live.

81.2.4.head: المَلا
81.2.4.meaning: An open stretch of barren country.

82.1.4.head: سِنان
82.1.4.meaning: A spearhead, here a figure for a warrior's sharpness.

83.2.5.head: مَأرَبَة
83.2.5.meaning: A need or purpose one seeks to fulfil.

84.2.4.head: جُذام
84.2.4.meaning: Judham, the Arab tribe in Syria to which Thabit ibn Nu'aym belonged.

85.1.3-4.head: أَسوَدُ سالِخ
85.1.3-4.meaning: “A black one shedding”, a black snake sloughing its skin.

85.2.1.head: حَتف
85.2.1.meaning: Death or a means of destruction, here plural.

86.2.4.head: أَدَبَ
86.2.4.meaning: To invite to a banquet. Here Death delivers the invitation.
